question: Who sets the prices of phone calls, video visits and commissary items in prisons and jails, and can the facility or sheriff keep a commission?

groups: Director of the Department of Corrections
Council of the District of Columbia

gold_sections.why: Phone providers may not charge more for operator-assisted calls from a D.C. penal or correctional institution than the Public Service Commission maximum, and no institution may charge a surcharge, commission or other financial imposition in addition to legally established phone rates.
The Public Service Commission must determine the maximum rate for operator-assisted calls from phones used by incarcerated residents.

Any District contract for holding or incarcerating people charged or convicted in Superior Court must ban surcharges and commissions in addition to legally established call rates; the District must seek quality service at least cost to the person paying for the call.
Commissary sales money goes into the Resident Welfare Fund, administered by the Director of the Department of Corrections; money left at fiscal year-end goes to the District's General Fund.
The Fund's uses in order of priority: stocking the commissaries, then goods and services benefiting the general resident population as the Committee decides.

The Resident Welfare Fund Committee (five Department of Corrections officials, including the Warden of the Central Detention Facility) administers and supervises the Fund's operations and spending, must record its approval of every expenditure, and may adopt regulations on the Fund's use.
Defines commissary, correctional facility (including facilities run under contract with the Department of Corrections), Department, Director and Fund.

The Department of Corrections, under the Mayor, has charge of managing the institutions it names, including the Washington Asylum and Jail, and with Council approval may make rules and regulations for their government; it must keep regular afternoon and evening visiting hours at the Central Detention Facility at least 5 days a week, including Saturdays and Sundays (the section does not say whether visits are in person or by video).

People serving D.C. Code felony sentences are designated to Bureau of Prisons facilities and are subject to federal law and regulation (by inference, federal rules rather than the D.C. Code govern their phone and commissary charges).

nuggets.text: No telephone service provider may charge a customer more for operator-assisted calls made from a penal or correctional institution in D.C. than the maximum rate set by the D.C. Public Service Commission, notwithstanding any other District law.
nuggets.quote: no telephone service provider shall charge a customer a rate for operator-assisted calls made from a penal or correctional institution in the District in excess of the maximum rate determined by the Public Service Commission of the District

nuggets.text: The Public Service Commission must determine the maximum rate for operator-assisted calls made from phones used by incarcerated residents of a D.C. penal or correctional institution.
nuggets.quote: The Public Service Commission shall determine the maximum rate for operator-assisted calls made from phones utilized by incarcerated residents of a penal or correctional institution in the District.

nuggets.text: No penal or correctional institution in D.C. may charge a surcharge, commission, or other financial imposition in addition to the legally established rates for local or long-distance telephone service.
nuggets.quote: No penal or correctional institution in the District shall charge a surcharge, commission, or other financial imposition that is in addition to legally established rates for local or long-distance telephone service.

nuggets.text: Any contract the District is a party to for holding or incarcerating people charged or convicted in D.C. Superior Court must prohibit surcharges, commissions, or other financial impositions in addition to the legally established rates for calls by incarcerated residents covered by the contract.
nuggets.quote: the contract shall prohibit surcharges, commissions, or other financial impositions that are in addition to the legally established rates for calls made by any incarcerated resident subject to the contract

nuggets.text: The District government must seek quality phone service at the least cost to the person who pays for an incarcerated resident's call.
nuggets.quote: The District government shall seek to obtain quality service for the least cost to the individual party paying for the telephone call by an incarcerated resident subject to the contract.

nuggets.text: A commissary is the system through which residents of District correctional facilities can buy permitted goods.
nuggets.quote: “Commissary” means a system through which residents in District correctional facilities are able to purchase permitted commodities.

nuggets.text: Money from selling goods through the commissary at correctional facilities must be deposited in the Resident Welfare Fund.
nuggets.quote: Monies derived from the sale of goods through the commissary at correctional facilities shall be deposited in the Fund.

nuggets.text: The Resident Welfare Fund is a special fund administered by the Director of the Department of Corrections under the uses set by 24-283.
nuggets.quote: There is established as a special fund the Resident Welfare Fund ("Fund"), which shall be administered by the Director of the Department of Corrections

nuggets.text: The Fund must be used in order of priority, first to stock the commissaries of District correctional facilities.
nuggets.quote: The Fund shall be used for the following purposes, in order of priority: (1) To stock the commissaries of District correctional

nuggets.text: After stocking the commissaries, the Fund pays for goods and services that benefit the general resident population of District correctional facilities, as the Resident Welfare Fund Committee decides.
nuggets.quote: To provide goods and services that benefit the general resident population at District correctional facilities, as determined by the Resident Welfare Fund Committee

nuggets.text: Any money left in the Fund at the end of a fiscal year is transferred to the unassigned balance of the District's General Fund.
nuggets.quote: Any money remaining available in the Fund at the end of a fiscal year, as determined by the Chief Financial Officer in the fiscal year-end close, shall be transferred to the unassigned fund balance of the General Fund of the District of Columbia

nuggets.text: The Resident Welfare Fund Committee, made up of five Department of Corrections officials, administers and supervises the Fund's operations and spending.
nuggets.quote: established for the purpose of administering and supervising the operations of and the expenditures from the Resident Welfare Fund

nuggets.text: The Department of Corrections, with the D.C. Council's approval, may promulgate rules and regulations for the government of the institutions 24-211.02(a) places in its charge, which include the Washington Asylum and Jail.
nuggets.quote: The Department of Corrections with the approval of the Council of the District of Columbia shall have power to promulgate rules and regulations for the government of such institutions

nuggets.text: The Department of Corrections must initiate and maintain regular afternoon and evening visiting hours at the Central Detention Facility (the D.C. Jail) for at least 5 days a week, including Saturdays and Sundays.
nuggets.quote: Initiate and maintain regular afternoon and evening visiting hours at the Central Detention Facility for a minimum of 5 days a week, including Saturdays and Sundays

nuggets.text: People serving D.C. Code felony sentences are designated by the Bureau of Prisons to facilities it operates or contracts for, and are subject to the laws and regulations that apply to people committed for violating federal law.
nuggets.quote: shall be designated by the Bureau of Prisons to a penal or correctional facility operated or contracted for by the Bureau of Prisons, for such term of imprisonment as the court may direct. Such persons shall be subject to any law or regulation applicable to persons committed for violations of laws of the United States consistent with the sentence imposed.

nuggets.text: Under the Mayor's general direction and supervision, the Department of Corrections has charge of managing and regulating the institutions the section names, including the Washington Asylum and Jail.
nuggets.quote: Said Department of Corrections under the general direction and supervision of the Mayor of the District of Columbia shall have charge of the management and regulation of the Workhouse at Occoquan in the State of Virginia, the Reformatory at Lorton in the State of Virginia, and the Washington Asylum and Jail

nuggets.text: The Resident Welfare Fund Committee may adopt regulations governing the use and spending of the Fund.
nuggets.quote: The Committee may promulgate regulations governing the use and expenditures of the Fund.

office.value: D.C. Public Service Commission: sets the maximum rate for operator-assisted calls from D.C. penal or correctional institutions
Department of Corrections (under the Mayor): manages the jail and, with D.C. Council approval, makes the rules for governing it
Director of the Department of Corrections: administers the Resident Welfare Fund that receives commissary sales money
Resident Welfare Fund Committee (Department of Corrections officials): supervises Fund spending, decides which goods and services benefit residents, and may issue regulations on Fund use
Federal Bureau of Prisons: designates people serving D.C. Code felony sentences to its facilities, where federal law and regulation apply

yes_no.value: phones: no add-on commission; a D.C. institution may not charge a surcharge or commission in addition to legally established phone rates, and District incarceration contracts must ban such add-ons (the Code does not expressly address revenue-sharing built into a vendor's rate); commissary: the sales revenue stays with the Department of Corrections in its Resident Welfare Fund, administered by the Director, for restocking and resident benefits, and any year-end balance goes to the District's General Fund

ordered_list.item: Commissary sales money is deposited in the Resident Welfare Fund
Next: goods and services benefiting the general resident population, as the Committee decides
Money left at fiscal year-end goes to the District's General Fund

answer: D.C. has no sheriffs; the Department of Corrections runs the jail [N16]. No phone company may charge more for operator-assisted calls from a D.C. jail or prison than the Public Service Commission's maximum rate [N1][N2]. No D.C. correctional institution may add a surcharge, commission or other charge on top of legally established phone rates [N3], and District contracts to hold people charged or convicted in Superior Court must ban such add-ons for calls [N4]; the District must seek quality service at least cost to the payer [N5]. The bans reach add-ons; the Code does not expressly address revenue-sharing built into rates. No statute sets commissary or video-visit prices. With Council approval, the Department makes rules governing the jail [N13]. It must keep afternoon and evening visiting hours at the Central Detention Facility (D.C. Jail) at least 5 days a week, including weekends [N14], though the statute does not say in person or by video. Commissary sales money stays in the Department's Resident Welfare Fund, run by the Corrections Director [N7][N8] and supervised by a committee of Department officials [N12] that may issue rules on Fund spending [N17]. The Fund first restocks the commissaries, then buys goods and services benefiting residents generally, as the committee decides [N9][N10]; any year-end balance goes to the District's General Fund [N11]. D.C. felony sentences are served in federal Bureau of Prisons facilities under federal law [N15]. Actual call, video and commissary prices and vendor payments come from FCC rules, PSC orders and DOC vendor contracts.

version_flags: 24-211.02: the corpus copy carries a note that it includes temporary-law amendments expiring September 11, 2026. The live D.C. Council page (code.dccouncil.gov, checked 2026-10-10, outside the corpus) instead notes emergency amendments expiring October 28, 2026, most recently D.C. Act 26-387 (July 30, 2026); all of these acts are titled 'Special Education for Young Adults in the Custody of the Department of Corrections' and concern only (b)(12), the special-education (FAPE) paragraph (the live text covers school years 2025-2026 and 2026-2027, the corpus 2024-2025 and 2025-2026), and the page says several have not been implemented pending funding. The permanent version (24-211.02(Perm)) ends at (b)(11) and has the same text as the corpus for the provisions relied on here, (a) (management and rulemaking) and (b)(3) (visiting hours), so the version question does not affect this answer.
notes: D.C. has no counties or sheriffs: the Department of Corrections (DOC) runs the Central Detention Facility (D.C. Jail) and the Correctional Treatment Facility, which hold pretrial detainees and sentenced misdemeanants; D.C. Code felons serve their time in Bureau of Prisons facilities under federal law (24-101), so the D.C. Code covers only the local facilities and District contracts. 24-101(a)'s text says 'any person who has been sentenced to incarceration pursuant to the District of Columbia Official Code', but its heading ('Felons sentences') and (b) concern felons; that federal rules govern BOP prisoners' phone and commissary charges is an inference from 'subject to any law or regulation applicable to persons committed for violations of laws of the United States'. 24-211.02(a) names the Occoquan Workhouse, the Lorton Reformatory and the Washington Asylum and Jail; reading its management and rulemaking power as covering today's D.C. Jail rests on that facility being the successor to the Washington Asylum and Jail, and 24-101(g)(1)(A) makes 24-211.02 inapplicable to functions the Bureau of Prisons took over. 24-211.02(b)(3) requires visiting hours at the Central Detention Facility only; it does not say whether visits are in person or by video, and no D.C. Code section mentions video visits. Phones: 24-263.01(a) and 24-263.04 tie only operator-assisted call rates to a Public Service Commission maximum; the statutes state no number. 24-263.01(b) bars an institution from charging a surcharge or commission 'in addition to legally established rates for local or long-distance telephone service'; it does not expressly address a site commission (a vendor paying the District a share of revenue built into the rate), and by its terms it is about telephone service, so it does not clearly reach video visits, tablets, electronic messaging or commissary markups. 24-263.02 requires the same add-on ban in District contracts 'for the holding or incarceration of persons' charged or convicted in Superior Court (for example, contracts to run a facility or house D.C. detainees); on its face it does not govern DOC's own contract with its phone or video vendor, and whether 'calls' includes video calls is not addressed. Site commissions are addressed by FCC rules (out of corpus). Possible tension: 34-2002(g) says the Public Service Commission shall not regulate rates of competitive telecommunications providers and 34-2006(c)(1) says Title 34, chapter 20 does not apply to the rates of VoIP or IP-enabled service (many modern jail phone systems). 24-263.01(a) opens 'Notwithstanding any other District law' and is specific to correctional institutions, which favors it, but chronology does not settle the question: 24-263.01 dates from D.C. Law 13-280 (2001) and was amended by D.C. Law 24-344 (2023), while the VoIP exemption in 34-2006(c) was added by D.C. Law 17-165 (2008), after the 2001 sections (history from code.dccouncil.gov; the corpus prints none). No statute resolves it. 24-263.03 (2001) required DOC to survey Bureau of Prisons and state prison communications plans, explore alternatives including commissary phone accounts and calling cards, and report on cost to families and the feasibility of waiving the gross receipts tax; it is a one-time report, not a rate rule. Commissary: no statute sets commissary prices or a markup cap. All monies 'derived from the sale of goods' through the commissary go to the Resident Welfare Fund (24-282(b)), so sales revenue stays with DOC's special fund, administered by the Director and spent with the approval of a Committee that includes the Warden of the Central Detention Facility, for restocking and resident benefits, but any year-end balance is swept to the General Fund (24-282(c)). 24-282(d) and (e) are repealed. 24-283 lists (1) and (3) in order of priority; (2) is repealed; the corpus text runs 'facilitiesand' together after (1). The Resident Welfare Fund Committee (24-284) has five members, all DOC officials (Director, General Counsel, Warden of the Central Detention Facility, the internal controls manager, and the IT director, or designees), must keep a record of its authorization and approval for all expenditures (24-284(c)), and may adopt regulations on the Fund's use (24-284(d)). 'Correctional facility' in 24-281 includes facilities run under contract with DOC. Juveniles: 2-1515.05a requires the Department of Youth Rehabilitation Services to give youth confidential telephone calls with the Public Defender Service's Juvenile Services Program but says nothing about prices. 1-325.21 (DOC Reimbursement Fund) concerns U.S. Marshals Service reimbursements and fees for housing federal and writ prisoners, not charges to residents.
